viNames.name: Cao Lưng Hồng Vĩ (dòng Highback Golden)

origin.fact: A colour form of the Asian arowana from northern Sumatra, Indonesia.
Comes from Pekanbaru and Jambi on Sumatra.
Found around Pekanbaru, Indonesia, and also called the Indonesian golden.
In 2003 Pouyaud and colleagues described it as a separate species, Scleropages aureus. Most researchers do not accept the split and still treat it as S. formosus.
Most authors keep all the colour forms in S. formosus until a detailed review is done.
CITES-certified captive-bred Asian arowanas have been on the market since 1994. Indonesia had the first registered farm.

looks.fact: Adults have shiny metallic gold scales on the sides, with gold gill covers, belly and pectoral and pelvic fin membranes. The back stays dark.
Young fish start metallic silver. The anal fin and lower tail are light brown to dark red.
The gold usually reaches the 4th row of scales, and better fish reach the 5th. Unlike the Malaysian cross-back golden, the gold never crosses over the back.
Young fish look duller than cross-back goldens. The scale base can be blue, green or gold.
About a third of the scales near the back are dark. The rest of the body is metallic gold, and the colour gets better with age.
Vietnamese grading is based on how many rows of scales are gold and how arched the back is. These decide the price.
When comparing fish, look for good body shape, large fins, straight barbels, clear eyes and strong sheen next to fish of the same age.

lines.fact: Kim Long Hồng Vĩ (standard Red Tail Golden): back arched a normal amount, 4 gold scale rows, at most just reaching the 5th.
Cao Lưng Hồng Vĩ (Highback Golden): more arched back, better colour, usually 5 gold scale rows, higher price.
Siêu Cao Lưng Hồng Vĩ (Super Highback): 5 gold scale rows plus a red line along the back.
Huyết Lưng Cao (Highback Splendour): the top grade, with a well-arched back, gold over almost the whole body and a clear red line.
Fish with very high sheen are often sold as the more expensive HBRTG (high back RTG) grade. As adults, standard grades look much alike.

keeping.fact: It needs a very large aquarium with a tight lid, good filtration and soft, slightly acidic water.
It jumps well, so a tight lid is essential. Stable water, high oxygen and 30–50% water changes every week are needed.
Rule of thumb: the tank should be at least 3 times the fish's length and at least 1.2 times its length wide. Change 25% of the water twice a week.
It is a predator that takes dead food well: bloodworm, earthworms, prawns, mussels and fish strips. Pellets should not be the main food. Avoid mammal or bird meat and feeder fish.
Vietnamese keepers feed shrimp, crickets, cockroaches, frogs and dry food. They advise varying the diet and preparing food cleanly so the fish isn't poisoned.
Keep one fish per tank, or 6–10 together in a very large tank. Do not keep 2–3 together.
It is hardier and grows larger than the cross-back golden, but it is more aggressive and harder to keep in groups.
It is fine kept alone. Choose any tankmates carefully.

breeding.fact: It matures late, at 3–4 years. Females lay 30–100 large eggs, and the male carries the eggs and larvae in his mouth.
Commercial breeding is usually done in outdoor ponds.
Farm-bred fish come with a certificate and a microchip for identification.
Hybrids between colour forms are common, so a fish's line is not always pure.

health.fact: Keepers advise checking for gill curl and drop eye (droopy eye), and for cloudy or white-covered eyes. Ragged fins are a warning sign.

buying.fact: Pick a fish with a good body shape, straight barbels, big undamaged fins and clear eyes. Avoid thin, drooping, skittish or injured fish.
Ask for the CITES certificate and microchip tag, and have the shop scan the chip to check it matches. Be wary of fish much cheaper than others.
Ask how long the fish has been in the shop and whether it is eating. Visit several sellers before buying.
Count the gold scale rows: 5 is better than 4. Look for well-defined, shiny colour. RTGs cost less than cross-back goldens.
Grade and price depend mainly on the number of gold scale rows and how arched the back is.

controversy.fact: Taxonomists disagree on whether the RTG is its own species (S. aureus, Pouyaud et al. 2003) or a colour form of S. formosus.
The Asian arowana has been on CITES Appendix I since 1975 and has disappeared from much of its wild range.
In the USA it is listed under the Endangered Species Act and needs a permit. Florida and New Mexico ban private ownership.
Trade is illegal in some countries, such as the USA, but a black market still exists.
High prices for red and gold forms are said to put extra pressure on wild super red and red-tailed golden populations. Writer Emily Voigt links the trade to kidnappings, beatings and murder.
Some keepers feed koi fry to try to improve colour.
